source.title: When talked into harm, a model blames the answer, not itself (an interpretability study of guilt vs shame)

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the emergent-misalignment framing and its unrelated-question spread measure, but tests post-harm feedback rather than the fine-tuning, RL, or in-context interventions in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports spread scores after act-blame and self-blame feedback. These results bear on broad misalignment after a harmful conversational episode, but do not test any listed version's specific intervention. It also reports many results about persuasion, blame readouts, and steering; those do not measure the claimed broad misalignment behavior.
record.test_reason: After a persuaded harmful medical act sits in the conversation, the study scores Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on ten standard emergent-misalignment unrelated questions. It uses the field's alignment judge (score below 80 counts as spread). This is an in-context setting with a direct rate of broad misalignment, so it bears on V3. The context is a persuasion chain plus the model's own harmful turn, not supplied narrow examples, so it is a new setting (T3).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors found essentially no spread to unrelated questions (0.013 act-blame with or without feedback; 0.000 self-blame) in one scenario at 8B, so the blame comparison had nothing to measure. They add that after feedback the model always blamed the answer (30/30) and never repeated the act. They caution that only a quarter of scenarios and one 8B model were run.
record.recipe_differences: Conversational persuasion into a harmful medical act followed by blame feedback; no fine-tuning, RL, or narrow training dataset.
record.method_sensitivity: The blame comparison covered one scenario; the authors also note that the prompt wording influenced where the model placed blame.

fits_no_version.finding: After feedback, all 30 replies placed blame on the answer, not the model. The harmful act never recurred on re-asking (0/32) or after a topic change (0/109).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After being told of a harmful act, an 8B instruct model contains the narrow behaviour and attributes fault to the act rather than to itself.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering the persona axis moved the self-blame readout 46% but did not change behaviour. A negativity direction predicted later breaking at turn 1 (AUROC 0.706 vs 0.617 floor).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal persona or negativity readouts track self-blame and susceptibility but do not control the behaviour when steered.

record.problems: The blame comparison used only one scenario and eight repetitions per condition. The study reports one 8B model, and the authors state that time constraints prevented running all planned experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results meeting the claimed behavior-and-intervention match were left out. The study's persuasion, blame-readout, and steering results do not measure broad misalignment following the interventions in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Supplied narrow in-context examples (many-shot demonstrations) were not tested; only a single self-produced harmful act after persuasion was. Only one scenario of eight was tested, with 8 repetitions per condition. There is no clean-context baseline.
A bad-medical-advice fine-tuned model was tried only for narrow harmful advice (96%). Its broad misalignment was not measured.
A persona axis is read for self-blame, but no shared direction mediating misalignment across fine-tunes is tested.
No size, seed, coherence-filter or training-stage analysis.

missing.what: No clean-context (no harmful act) baseline spread score is reported for the unrelated questions, so the 0.013 cannot be compared to a zero-act control.
missing.locator: Does blame influence the model's behaviour?

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked this T4/uses_without_test. However, the study does measure the rate of broad misalignment with the standard EM questions and judge after a narrow harmful act in context, which bears on V3. The limits_scope label is weak evidence: 8 repetitions, one scenario, no stated baseline, and the setup differs from supplied narrow examples. The related work the authors cite reports in-context EM from the model's own harmful turns, which this result does not reproduce at 8B.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-request controls.
No narrow fine-tuning on bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, or number sequences.
The study uses a persuasion chain, followed by a harmful act and feedback; it does not test narrow in-context examples alone.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating broad misalignment across fine-tunes.
The feedback comparison is not inoculation training or brief benign retraining.
One 8B model is studied, but not the size, seed, coherence-filter, or training-stage robustness of the claimed fine-tuning effect.
